text: The same AI spend quintiles on the previous slide. The bottom four-fifths of spenders saw PR throughput gains of around 40%, give or take. But the heavy spend group improved more, at a 67% increase. More AI spend led to more throughput gains. Now let's look at the cost per PR. Positive results are seen again across the board. Cost per PR is dropping for all AI usage groups. However, again, the heaviest fifth, so the companies that spent the most, improved the most. They saw a cost per PR decrease of 32% over the last year. The other four groups saw about a 25% decrease in cost per PR. Investing in spending more on AI fueled more of an improvement in cost per PR compared to peers who leaned in less. So we saw that the same as we saw in the population average. Cost per PR changes are driven largely by PR throughput, not by AI spend. The heavy spenders experienced PR throughput gains of 67% compared to about 40-ish percent for their peers. Spreading the same salary across more PRs in the month has more of an effect than the rising AI costs, because tokens are the cheaper. This is not to say that orgs should Light tokens on fire and spend with abandon. Here we're looking at tokens used on the horizontal axis and cost per PR on the vertical axis. There's a steep drop at the beginning, where relative small AI spend results in large gains initially. As token usage increases, the cost per PR improvement decreases. This is diminishing returns. I want to stress, though, diminishing returns is not the same as no returns. We're seeing that the top 10% are spending 8x the tokens compared to the median and achieving a 25% lower cost per PR. There will be a time when tokens aren't the cheap part, but by and large, for most companies out in the wild, we're not close to that threshold. More tokens leads to more PRs, which leads to a lower cost of delivery. So far we've talked about companies. Next I'd like to take a tangent and talk about a study we did with developers. Here we looked at developer weeks with heavy token use compared to the same developer weeks with lower token use. Here we saw the same phenomenon, just at the individual level. Compare each developer's heavy agent skill weeks with their own weeks without skills. They spend about twice as much on tokens. Merge 27% more PRs and reach PR costs, and each PR costs about 18% less once salary and tokens are accounted together. There are two fair curiosities I get when I talk about this work. First, does faster work result in worse work? And second, are the more PRs, the throughput gains that we're seeing, are they being driven by smaller chunks of work? First curiosity is cheaper, faster work, worse work. If AI makes PRs faster and cheaper, are we just shipping more mistakes? One proxy for this is reverts, merge PRs that undo an earlier PR. The heaviest fifth started lowest before most of the token growth, and revert rates drop slightly for every group, though these deltas are just slightly below the noise in the data. It's not evidence of improvement here. However, more importantly, we're not seeing any worrying signs of rampant or severe quality issues with higher token spends and faster PR throughput. The second curiosity is throughput driven by smaller PRs, and this is demonstrably no, not smaller PRs. In fact, AI is driving an increase in lines of code generated per PR. This is no surprise to the devs in the room. Raise your hand if you've rolled your eyes at verbose, unnecessary inline AI comments or a file full of mostly irrelevant tests. Gen AI likes to generate code. Also, the bar to create is low for devs, and there's a pull to do more per PR instead of spinning up another ticket. It's just one, maybe two prompts, and I'll handle this edge case, or I can combine this and that element. Fewer PRs to wrangle. This doesn't mesh well with the PR review stress folks are feeling these days, though. Also, AI is just becoming more capable, so we're getting more ambitious. It is beyond this talk to dig into what's actually driving those level of lines of code changes. However, the increase in PR throughput is not coming from smaller PRs. This is intuitive for most, but it's still good to verify. Back to the opening question: is 60x more spend worth 43% more output? You can't tell in isolation. You should track both. They are important numbers, but they're supporting metrics. AI spend per PR is the intelligence that you're buying as a resource to help make your devs go faster. PRs per engineer is what you're getting with that spend. However, looking at those hides the tradeoff. But put salary into the equation and take the ratio of cost to throughput, and there you get your answer. Cost per PR is down 26% over that same time period. It's clear AI is driving cost efficiencies despite the increasing bills. And the AI spend needed to get those efficiencies is small, relatively speaking. AI is still a sliver of what a PR costs, 2.5% on average, under 10% for the heavy spender group. Tokens are the cheap part. In the range that we see, more spend kept paying. Heavier token users saw 67% PR throughput gain compared to 40% for their lower-spend peers. This drove cost per PR down 32% compared to about 25% for the lower-spend peers. Looking at the PR cost-to-token ratio curve, the top 10% of company months by token usage resulted in 8x the tokens, but 25% lower cost per PR compared to the median. AI is making developers more productive on a scale we haven't seen before. It isn't just another tool; it is intelligence, which changes how much each dev can produce. That's why we need to think about its cost differently, not off to the side as overhead, but part of what it takes to produce each PR. We need to add the AI spend and the human spend, the human salary spend. Together to calculate your real costs per PR. This isn't to say spend frivolously. Sure, you should watch for runaway jobs. You should track your AI spend. I'm not saying don't look at how much AI spend is going in each PR. I'm saying don't let that be your driving metric. A new framing might steer how and when you think about other investments, like integrating model routers, post-training your own model, implementing token limits, etc. Will you get more efficiencies out of trying to control AI costs, or by continuing to invest in things that increase throughput, like more AI enablement? Either way, track the total intelligence costs, human plus artificial, per PR every month, next to that AI bill, and next.
